chapters.title: The Deduction Board

lines.text: The aquarium reopens on Monday. The tanks are full, the sharks are calm, and the breeding records — for the first time in years — are true.
And in the feeding log, tucked between the pages, one more thing the police never logged: a small black envelope, sealed with a silver anchor.
Glass, salt water, and the low hum of the pumps. The aquarium is beautiful after dark — and tonight, it is a crime scene.
Dr. Lena Marsh loved the sea. She counted its creatures the way other people count money — and she found the numbers did not add up.
The aquarium called it an accident. Her tea cup disagrees. You are the detective the Cold Case Unit sends when the obvious answer is too tidy.

premise: Dr. Lena Marsh, curator of the Port Anselm Aquarium, is found dead in the back of the shark gallery on a Friday night — drowned in the quarantine tank, her tea cup still warm on the lab bench. The aquarium calls it a terrible accident. The tea cup says otherwise: it holds a veterinary sedative, and the tank holds the same drug, at the same concentration. Someone counted the specimens the way Marsh did, found the same gap, and decided she would never tell the board on Monday.

solve.solutionHTML:
Dana Whitfield drugged Lena Marsh's tea with a veterinary sedative taken from the clinic — her keycard opened the clinic at 21:05 — then carried the unconscious woman to the quarantine tank and staged a drowning, looping the cameras for the thirty minutes she needed. Her fingerprint, lifted from the hinge side of the tank lid where her wipe missed, is the last link. The motive is the manifest: four rare specimens sold to a private collector, the grant money following them, and Marsh's unsent email — 'I am telling the board on Monday.' The audit letter that arrived that morning meant Dana was about to be exposed by two people at once.

No single clue convicts her. The print alone could be innocent — she manages the building. The keycard alone proves a clinic visit, not a murder. The sedative alone proves a drugging, not a killer. Together, they leave no one else: only Dana had the keycard, the manifest, the buyer on her second phone, and the reason to silence the one woman who had done the sums.

suspects.secret: He has been selling old aquarium equipment — pumps, nets, a wetsuit — online, a little at a time, for rent money.
suspects.trustIntro: Defensive, then relieved when the listings are read properly. He is a small thief, not a killer.
truthList: I sold equipment, yes — old pumps, a spare net. Not specimens.
I was home by nine. Alone. I know.
I have never been in the clinic, and I have never touched that tank.

title: The Glass Tide

twists.body: The sedative log's sign-out handwriting is not the vet's — and Rosa admits the clinic's keycard reader has been broken for a month, so anyone with a staff card could have walked in unlogged. The keycard record suddenly proves less than it seemed — until you check whose card was used, and when.
twists.title: The broken keycard reader

twists.body: The second phone's call log shows the buyer was called twice on the night Marsh died — but the second call was made after the murder, from the loading dock. Dana did not just kill Marsh. She finished the shipment that night, while the body was still warm in the tank room. And the buyer's number matches a name the Unit already knows — a name that will matter in Case 6.
twists.title: The second call
